_about: Raw measured data for the optimization writeup. Every value here was measured, not estimated. Fields prefixed with _ are notes, not data. Do not quote a number from this file without its accompanying caveat.

asset_pipeline._method: File sizes via stat. Triangle counts, texture size and GPU memory via @gltf-transform/core reading each stage. GPU memory = sum of accessor byte lengths + (texture width * height * 4 * 4/3) for the mip chain. gzip via node:zlib level 6.
asset_pipeline._gpu_note: GPU memory is independent of file size. Encoded textures (JPEG/WebP) are decoded to raw RGBA on upload, so a small file can still cost a lot of VRAM.

stages._note: No change. dedup had already removed everything unreferenced.

Requested ratio 0.5 but delivered only -5.3%. The 1% error bound stopped it: hard architectural surfaces have little redundant geometry to give up. The bound protected building silhouettes, which is the correct outcome.

asset_pipeline._gzip_caveat: IMPORTANT FRAMING. The source gzips to 25.32 MB because the ~472 MB of duplicate buffer data compresses away almost entirely. The honest over-the-wire comparison is therefore 25.32 MB vs 6.24 MB (-75.4%), NOT 519 vs 8.42. A '98% smaller' claim partly measures redundancy that any HTTP compression would have caught on its own.
asset_pipeline._gzip_anomaly: Stage 1 gzips LARGER than the source (26.37 vs 25.32 MB). dedup removed redundancy that gzip was already exploiting, so the bytes that remain are denser. Real effect, not a measurement error.

codec_comparison._method: Both built from the same stage-6 input and measured with stat.
codec_comparison._decision: Draco is 65.6% smaller, far more than the 'marginally smaller' the PRD anticipated. Meshopt was still chosen: the 5.5 MB difference is under a second of extra download, while Draco's decode runs on the main thread and risks stalling the first frame on weak hardware. Measuring the alternative and rejecting it for a stated reason is part of the result.

parse_cost._method: Node, bytes preloaded into memory so only the parse is timed. Relative decode comparison, NOT a prediction of browser timings.
parse_cost._note: Optimized figure includes meshopt WASM decode.

load_timings._method: Browser Performance API via window.__cityMetrics, DevTools cache disabled. Measured against the VITE DEV SERVER.
load_timings._caveat: Dev-server numbers. documentLoadMs and domContentLoadedMs are badly inflated by Vite serving hundreds of unbundled ES modules, which production does not do. Re-measure on `npm run preview` before publishing these two fields. timeToInteractiveMs and the model request are more representative.
load_timings._compression_caveat: transferredMb equals decodedMb in both runs because the Vite dev server does not compress. Netlify gzips, so the real transfer is ~6.24 MB, about 26% less than measured here.

runtime._method: Custom PerfHUD reading WebGLRenderer.info. Draw calls and triangles are the renderer's own per-frame counts, not estimates. Sampled while orbiting.
runtime._triangle_discrepancy: HUD reports 319,610 vs 318,648 in the file. The extra ~962 is the ocean plane, sky dome and the model's LINES primitive. The HUD counts what is submitted per frame; the file count is city geometry only. Both correct, different questions.
runtime._honesty_note: CRITICAL FRAMING - DO NOT OVERCLAIM. The unoptimized model loaded in 4-5s and still held 117 FPS, because it was served from a local SSD with no network involved. The optimization did NOT rescue a broken frame rate; the frame rate was never broken on this hardware. Frame rate improved 117 -> ~143 FPS, which is real but secondary. The genuine wins are DELIVERY (519 MB is ~7 minutes at 10 Mbps and effectively undeliverable on mobile) and GPU MEMORY (122.77 -> 35.71 MB), which is what protects weaker hardware than this test machine.

texel_density._method: Per-triangle world area vs UV area gives linear texel density; converted to screen pixels per texel at a given camera distance. Above 1.0 the texture is magnified and reads soft.
texel_density._decision: 1024 was rejected: even the default wide shot sat at 4.72 px/texel and rendered crops showed facades turning to mush. 4096 was rejected: 11.05 MB and 89.48 MB GPU, handing back the entire texture-memory win for detail a single city-wide atlas cannot resolve at any resolution.
